One-page synthesis

Core thesis. Despite widespread psychotropic use in BPD, the review found no consistent evidence that pharmacotherapy alone reduces overall BPD severity. Possible benefits were symptom-specific, usually supported by low- or very-low-certainty evidence, while second-generation antipsychotics showed a small increase in overall adverse events and no demonstrated functional benefit.
What the evidence contains21 RCTs, mostly placebo-controlled; second-generation antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, and fluoxetine; only 9 of 87 eligible drugs.
Strongest negative signalLamotrigine did not improve BPD severity in the relatively large LABILE trial; overall class evidence did not consistently improve core BPD severity.
Potential symptom signalsLow/very-low-certainty single-study signals for anger, aggression, and affective lability with some anticonvulsants; antipsychotics may improve general psychopathology.
HarmsAntipsychotic adverse events: 67% vs 60%, pooled RR 1.10 (95% CI 1.00-1.21). Serious-harm evidence was sparse.
Evidence fragility12 of 21 RCTs were high risk of bias; attrition reached 68%; most studies were small and short; populations were mostly female and white.
Best useEvidence framing for why medication should not be expected to treat BPD globally and why symptom-targeted pharmacotherapy claims require caution.

Section condensation

Abstract

The review asked whether pharmacological treatments improve borderline personality disorder (BPD), specific BPD-associated symptoms, general psychiatric symptoms, functioning, and harms. The abstract reports searches through April 6, 2021 and 21 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 1768 participants, covering only nine of 87 prespecified medications.

The abstract concludes that second-generation antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, and antidepressants did not consistently reduce overall BPD severity. It characterizes possible symptom-specific benefits of anticonvulsants as low-certainty and largely single-study evidence, while second-generation antipsychotics showed limited symptom effects but some improvement in general psychiatric symptoms.

1 Introduction

The introduction frames BPD as a chronic, functionally impairing disorder with frequent psychiatric comorbidity, self-harm, suicidality, and high service use. It notes that psychotherapy is generally positioned as first-line treatment and that no medication is approved specifically for BPD, despite extensive psychotropic use and frequent polypharmacy.

The rationale for the review is a mismatch between common medication use and an evidence base last comprehensively assessed in an older Cochrane review. The review was intended to inform American Psychiatric Association guideline development and to evaluate both general efficacy and comparative effectiveness of pharmacotherapy.

2 Methods

The review followed AHRQ effectiveness-review methods and PRISMA-related reporting, with protocol registration in PROSPERO (CRD42020194098). The key questions covered efficacy, comparative effectiveness, harms, and subgroup differences by age, gender, race/ethnicity, or genotype.

The analytic framework linked pharmacological interventions in diagnosed BPD to intermediate and health outcomes, while separately capturing discontinuation and adverse effects. The methods distinguish study-level risk of bias from body-of-evidence certainty.

2.1 Literature Searches

An earlier APA search through December 2017 was supplemented with MEDLINE, EMBASE, the Cochrane Library, and PsycINFO searches from January 1, 2018 through April 6, 2021. Searches were limited to English-language and human studies, and reference lists of landmark studies and background articles were manually searched.

The supplement provides the exact database strategies and search dates. This supports reproducibility of the retrieval process, although the English-language restriction is a stated limitation.

2.2 Criteria for Inclusion/Exclusion

Eligible participants were age 13 years or older, from very-high-human-development-index countries, with BPD diagnosed by DSM-IV/DSM-5 or ICD-10 criteria. Included interventions spanned anticonvulsants, antidepressants, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, melatonin, opioid agonists/antagonists, and sedative-hypnotics, with at least eight weeks of treatment.

Eligible comparators were placebo or another eligible medication. Prespecified outcomes included overall BPD severity, individual symptoms such as aggression, anger and self-harm, general psychiatric symptoms, functioning, and adverse outcomes. The supplement expands these criteria and lists the 87 prespecified pharmacotherapies.

2.3 Literature Review, Data Abstraction, and Data Management

Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full-text articles, resolving disagreement by consensus or a senior reviewer. Studies identified in the earlier APA search were rescreened against the current eligibility criteria.

A structured DistillerSR form was pilot tested for extraction. One reviewer extracted study data and a second team member verified accuracy and completeness; this is a verification model rather than fully independent duplicate extraction.

2.4 Assessment of Risk of Bias

Two independent reviewers used Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 and could rate risk at the outcome level when limitations differed by outcome. High risk was assigned when design or conduct limitations were serious enough to threaten validity.

Disagreements were resolved by discussion and consensus or a third reviewer. Supplementary Figure 1 displays the domain-level judgments and shows that missing outcome data was a recurrent problem.

2.5 Data Synthesis

Studies were synthesized narratively unless populations, interventions, comparators, and outcomes were sufficiently similar for pooling. Meta-analyses used restricted-maximum-likelihood random-effects models; clinical and methodological heterogeneity were assessed before pooling, and statistical heterogeneity was examined with chi-square and I-squared statistics.

The authors used sensitivity analyses for potential heterogeneity and reverted to narrative synthesis when pooling was not appropriate because of heterogeneity, sparse studies, or incompatible outcome reporting.

2.6 Grading the Certainty of Evidence

The review used GRADE to rate certainty across risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and reporting bias, with optional consideration of factors such as magnitude of association and dose-response relationships.

Two reviewers assessed GRADE domains and resolved differences by consensus; decisions to upgrade or downgrade were documented. Supplementary Table 5 supplies outcome-specific certainty ratings and anticipated absolute effects.

2.7 Role of the Funding Source

The American Psychiatric Association funded the review. Its Clinical Guidelines Committee assisted in developing the key questions, inclusion criteria, and outcomes of interest.

The source explicitly states that the APA committee was not involved in data collection, analysis, or manuscript preparation. The funding relationship remains relevant because the review was designed to support APA guideline development.

3 Results - Evidence Base

The Results section reports 14,797 unique records and 21 included RCTs in 24 publications; no eligible observational studies were found. Nineteen RCTs were placebo-controlled and two were active-comparator trials. The evidence covered second-generation antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, and one second-generation antidepressant, representing only nine of 87 drugs of interest.

Across 1768 participants, 79% were female and 76% were white when race was reported; follow-up ranged from 8 to 52 weeks. Two studies were rated low risk of bias, seven moderate, and 12 high, with high attrition the major driver of high-risk ratings. The source contains a record-count inconsistency: the abstract reports 12,062 unique records, whereas the Results section reports 14,797.

3.1 Second-Generation Antipsychotics versus Placebo

Nine double-blind RCTs contributed 1124 participants. Most trials assessed olanzapine, with single trials of aripiprazole, quetiapine extended release, and ziprasidone. Follow-up ranged from 8 weeks to 6 months; all but one trial were industry-funded.

Overall BPD-severity findings were mixed and the review rated certainty as low for no effect of assessed second-generation antipsychotics on overall BPD severity. Symptom-level effects were inconsistent across depression, anger, impulsiveness, aggression, and self-harm.

3.1.1 Severity of BPD

Two olanzapine trials produced mixed findings on the Zanarini Rating Scale for BPD: one flexible-dose arm showed greater improvement than placebo, while other olanzapine comparisons did not. A quetiapine extended-release trial reported improvement for the 150 mg/day arm but not the 300 mg/day arm, without reporting a treatment-effect estimate.

Because findings were inconsistent and several studies were high risk of bias, the review judged the body of evidence as low certainty for no overall antipsychotic effect on BPD severity.

3.1.2 Severity of BPD-Associated Symptoms

A five-study random-effects meta-analysis in 497 participants found no statistically significant reduction in depressive symptoms with second-generation antipsychotics versus placebo (standardized mean difference 0.28, 95% CI -0.05 to 0.60). One aripiprazole trial reported improved anger, while other symptom domains were inconsistent or negative.

The review rated evidence as low for an aripiprazole benefit on anger and for a quetiapine-ER benefit on aggression, and low for no effect of other assessed antipsychotics on depression, impulsiveness, aggression, and self-harm.

3.1.3 General Psychopathology and Functioning

Several trials found greater improvement on global psychopathology scales such as SCL-90-R or Clinical Global Impression with aripiprazole, olanzapine, or quetiapine compared with placebo, while other small high-risk-of-bias trials did not.

The review rated certainty as moderate for a beneficial effect on general psychopathology and moderate for no effect on functioning. This distinction is important: improvements in global psychiatric symptom scales did not translate into demonstrated functional benefit.

3.1.4 Adverse Events and Withdrawals

Adverse events were generally more frequent with second-generation antipsychotics. The pooled estimate was 67% versus 60% with placebo, RR 1.10 (95% CI 1.00-1.21), with common events including dry mouth, constipation, dizziness, sedation, and weight gain.

The review rated certainty as moderate for a higher overall adverse-event risk and low for similar withdrawal-due-to-adverse-event risk. The supplementary withdrawal meta-analysis was imprecise (RR 1.91, 95% CI 0.83-4.43), and serious-adverse-event data were too sparse for reliable inference.

3.2 Anticonvulsants versus Placebo

Nine double-blind RCTs of divalproex sodium, lamotrigine, or topiramate contributed 523 participants. Two studies were low risk, three moderate risk, and four high risk; four trials were industry-funded and the remaining trials reported no funding or government/university support.

The strongest evidence for overall BPD severity came from the publicly funded LABILE trial of lamotrigine, which found no significant difference at 52 weeks. Other anticonvulsant evidence was small and often high risk of bias.

3.2.1 Severity of BPD

The LABILE trial (N=276) and a smaller lamotrigine RCT found no significant difference in BPD severity versus placebo. A small divalproex trial likewise found no significant difference on the Borderline Evaluation of Severity Over Time scale.

The review rated certainty as moderate for no effect of lamotrigine and very low for no effect of divalproex sodium on overall BPD severity.

3.2.2 BPD-Associated Symptoms

Small trials reported reductions in anger with divalproex, lamotrigine, and topiramate; one divalproex trial also reported an aggression difference, and a small lamotrigine trial reported improved affective lability. These findings came from small studies with substantial risk of bias.

The review rated evidence as low for divalproex, lamotrigine, and topiramate on anger, very low for divalproex on aggression, and very low for lamotrigine on affective lability. The authors explicitly caution that chance findings are plausible.

3.2.3 General Psychopathology and Functioning

One low-risk-of-bias RCT in 56 women found greater improvement in general psychopathology with topiramate than placebo (7.4 vs 1.8 on the SCL-90-R Global Severity Index; p<0.001). Other trials did not demonstrate functional improvement with lamotrigine or divalproex.

The review rated certainty as low for topiramate improving general psychopathology, moderate for no effect of lamotrigine on social functioning, and very low for no effect of divalproex on social functioning.

3.2.4 Adverse Events and Withdrawals

Divalproex and topiramate trials did not report usable incidence data for adverse or serious adverse events. Lamotrigine trials reported similar adverse-event and serious-adverse-event incidence to placebo.

The anticonvulsant withdrawal meta-analysis showed no statistically significant difference versus placebo (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.12-1.89). Certainty was low for similar lamotrigine adverse-event risk and very low for withdrawal risk across anticonvulsants.

3.3 Antidepressants versus Placebo

One published, industry-funded, high-risk-of-bias RCT (N=25) compared fluoxetine with placebo while all participants received dialectical behavior therapy. An unpublished trial (N=75) tested fluoxetine or placebo added to dialectical behavior therapy or supportive psychotherapy in patients with BPD and suicidal behavior or self-mutilation.

The published trial did not assess overall BPD severity or adverse-event incidence. The unpublished trial had insufficient methodological information for formal risk-of-bias assessment.

3.3.1 Symptoms and 3.3.2 Functioning

The published fluoxetine trial found no significant difference in anger or aggression after 12 weeks. ClinicalTrials.gov data for the unpublished trial did not show a statistically significant difference in suicide attempts between groups with and without fluoxetine.

No functioning difference was detected in the published trial. The review rated certainty as very low for no effect of fluoxetine on anger, aggression, and functioning.

3.4 Second-Generation Antipsychotics versus Antidepressants

One 8-week, industry-funded, moderate-risk-of-bias RCT (N=45; all women) compared olanzapine, fluoxetine, and their combination. It did not report overall BPD severity, general psychiatric symptoms, or adverse-event incidence.

Olanzapine alone and olanzapine plus fluoxetine produced greater improvements in aggression and depressive symptoms than fluoxetine alone. The review rated certainty as low for these comparative symptom effects and very low for similar withdrawal-due-to-adverse-event risk.

3.5 Second-Generation Antipsychotics versus Second-Generation Antipsychotics

One 12-week open-label randomized trial (N=51), rated high risk of bias, compared asenapine with olanzapine. Funding was not reported, and the study did not report general psychiatric symptoms or functioning.

No significant differences were detected for BPD severity, aggression, impulsiveness, or self-harm; adverse-event and withdrawal incidence were similar. The review rated these comparisons as very low certainty.

4 Discussion

The discussion interprets the evidence as showing limited pharmacotherapy efficacy for BPD overall. Antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, and antidepressants did not consistently reduce core BPD severity; anticonvulsants had possible symptom-specific benefits supported mostly by low- or very-low-certainty single-study evidence, while antipsychotics showed some benefit on general psychopathology but not functioning.

The authors emphasize the fragility and limited generalizability of the evidence: only nine of 87 medications were studied; only four of 21 RCTs enrolled more than 70 participants; attrition reached 68%; most follow-up was 8-12 weeks; participants were mostly female and white; adolescents and prespecified subgroups were not studied; common psychiatric comorbidities were usually excluded; no large long-term observational studies were eligible; and publication/reporting bias could not be excluded.

5 Conclusions

The authors conclude that only low-quality evidence is available to guide pharmacotherapy for BPD. Benefits appear limited to selected individual symptoms rather than the disorder overall, and even symptom-specific evidence is generally low certainty.

They call for adequately powered, low-bias trials that examine clinically important subgroups and patient-relevant outcomes such as social functioning and meaningful symptom improvement.

Declarations and Data Availability

The authors declared no potential conflicts of interest. The work was funded by the American Psychiatric Association, with open-access funding from Danube University Krems University for Continuing Education.

Data for meta-analyses were stated to be available upon request; code availability was not applicable. The article is distributed under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial 4.0 license.

Figure 1 - Analytic framework

The framework starts with diagnosed BPD patients aged at least 13 years and links pharmacological interventions to intermediate outcomes, health outcomes, and treatment discontinuation/adverse effects. The framework supports the review's separation of efficacy, function, and harms.

Figure 2 - Literature search and selection

The flow diagram shows 2,853 records screened in the update process, 2,692 excluded at screening, 161 full-text articles assessed, 140 full-text exclusions, and 21 included studies in 24 publications. The prior APA search is shown separately with 12,062 screened records and 115 included records feeding the update.

Table 2 - Characteristics and risk of bias of included studies

This multi-page table is the primary study inventory. It reports study design, funding, sample size, intervention/dose, duration, population/setting, demographics, primary outcome, and risk-of-bias rating for the 21 included RCTs. The embedded pages are rotated for readability.

Pattern: studies were generally small; most participants were adults; many trials were industry-funded; risk-of-bias ratings ranged from low to high, with high attrition prominent.

Figure 3 - Depressive symptoms, antipsychotics versus placebo

Five studies contributed 497 participants. Pooled standardized mean difference was 0.28 (95% CI -0.05 to 0.60), with I² 57.66% and p=0.10 for the pooled effect. The confidence interval crosses no effect.

Figure 4 - Incidence of adverse events, antipsychotics versus placebo

Four studies produced RR 1.10 (95% CI 1.00-1.21), with I² 0%. The main text describes 67% versus 60% event incidence and rates this as moderate-certainty evidence for a small higher adverse-event risk.

Evaluation and appraisal

Verdict: Read soon. The review is methodologically useful and directly relevant to BPD pharmacotherapy, but the underlying evidence is weak, narrow, and now temporally dated. It is best used to understand why broad pharmacotherapy claims are unsupported, not as a current stand-alone practice standard.
Relevance8/10

Directly addresses efficacy and harms of medications commonly used in BPD.

Evidence basis: 21 RCTs across major psychotropic classes.

Limiting factor: only nine of 87 drugs had controlled evidence.

Would rise: a current update with newer trials and guideline linkage.

Novelty7/10

At publication, it updated an older evidence base with formal RoB 2 and GRADE assessment.

Evidence basis: authors describe it as the largest attempt to date and include 2018-2021 updates.

Limiting factor: several conclusions reproduce long-standing uncertainty rather than establish new efficacy.

Would rise: new comparative or subgroup evidence that changes treatment expectations.

Method strength8/10

Protocol registration, multi-database searching, dual screening, dual RoB assessment, GRADE, and random-effects synthesis are strong review methods.

Evidence basis: PROSPERO registration; AHRQ/PRISMA framework; RoB 2; GRADE; REML meta-analysis.

Limiting factor: English-only eligibility and extraction by one reviewer with verification rather than independent duplicate extraction.

Would rise: broader language coverage, duplicate extraction, and fully reconciled record counts.

Evidence strength4/10

The synthesis is careful, but the underlying treatment evidence is mostly low or very low certainty.

Evidence basis: 12 of 21 RCTs high risk; sparse pooling; many single-study symptom findings; small samples.

Limiting factor: high attrition, imprecision, short follow-up, inconsistent outcomes.

Would rise: adequately powered, low-bias, replicated trials with patient-centered outcomes.

External validity3/10

Applicability to routine BPD populations is restricted.

Evidence basis: 79% female; 76% white when reported; no adolescent trials; common psychiatric comorbidities usually excluded.

Limiting factor: narrow trial populations and mostly short treatment periods.

Would rise: diverse pragmatic cohorts, comorbid populations, adolescents, and long-term follow-up.

Implementation value7/10

Useful for setting expectations and preventing overinterpretation of symptom-targeted medication use.

Evidence basis: explicit outcome-by-outcome GRADE judgments, study inventory, harms synthesis, and clear evidence gaps.

Limiting factor: does not provide a validated medication algorithm and predates later evidence.

Would rise: updated comparative-effectiveness data tied to current guidance and specific decision pathways.

Systematic-review-specific appraisal

DomainAssessment
SearchFour major databases plus reference-list searching; exact strategies in supplement; English-language restriction.
SelectionDual independent screening with consensus/third-reviewer resolution.
ExtractionStructured form; one extractor plus verification. Adequate, but not the strongest duplicate-extraction design.
Risk of biasCochrane RoB 2 with two reviewers; major limitation is the poor quality of many included trials.
CertaintyGRADE used systematically and transparently; most clinically interesting effects remain low/very low certainty.
Meta-analysisREML random effects with heterogeneity assessment; pooling appropriately limited by sparse/heterogeneous evidence.
Publication biasAcknowledged as unquantifiable; sparse evidence limits formal assessment.
ApplicabilityPoor for adolescents, men, non-white populations, common comorbidities, long-term treatment, and rare serious harms.
Principal evidence limitation. High-quality evidence is not merely absent for many comparisons; for most prespecified medications there is no controlled evidence at all. The review's strongest conclusion is therefore about uncertainty and lack of consistent efficacy, not proof that every medication is ineffective in every BPD patient.

Confidence in appraisal: High for appraisal of this source because the full article and 47-page supplement were inspected, including main and supplementary figures/tables. Moderate for contemporary clinical relevance because the search ended in April 2021.

Practice / implementation takeaways

What this source supportsDo not expect pharmacotherapy alone to produce reliable improvement in overall BPD severity. Treat symptom-specific signals as uncertain unless supported by stronger replicated evidence.
What it does not supportA class-wide claim that antipsychotics, anticonvulsants, or antidepressants are effective treatments for the BPD syndrome as a whole.
Safety implicationSecond-generation antipsychotics carry a small pooled increase in overall adverse events; serious-event and withdrawal estimates are too sparse or imprecise for strong conclusions.
Evidence-selection implicationWhen using individual trial findings from this review, read the primary RCT directly before treating the finding as primary evidence. The review is a secondary source.
Research priorityLarge, low-bias trials with diverse populations, common comorbidities, longer follow-up, and patient-centered functional outcomes.
Current-use constraintBefore applying to 2026 practice, update the evidence search and compare with current clinical guidance.
